strengths: Technically sound and well-motivated framework: the <ANCHOR> token elegantly replaces the impractical aggregation over all query tokens, and the visual-sink query token mechanism for attention head weighting is a novel, interpretable idea grounded in attention-head analysis literature (semantic heads, induction heads).

Strong empirical results: GUI-AIMA-3B achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B models on ScreenSpot-Pro (45.2 base, 58.6 with zoom-in) and OSWorld-G (62.2 with zoom-in), rivaling or exceeding 7B models (UI-TARS-1.5-7B, JEDI-7B, GUI-Actor-7B), with notable gains on icon-centric tasks.

Excellent data and training efficiency: one-stage fine-tuning on ~85k screenshots / 259k samples, no extra grounding modules, no warm-up stage, and fastest convergence (Fig. 4) compared to vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor — a convincing demonstration that light training can elicit native grounding capability.

Thorough ablation study (Table 4) that isolates each design choice (anchor token, head-weighting schemes, global vs. layer-wise Qs selection, top-K, weighted patch labels), plus a dedicated appendix analysis (Fig. 5) supporting the hidden-state-based visual-sink token selection.

The coordinate-free patch-wise formulation naturally supports a plug-and-play two-step zoom-in inference, and Section 4.3 / Table 5 provide an honest error analysis (Recovered/Lost statistics, sensitivity to zoom factor) rather than only reporting headline numbers.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness concerns: the '+ zoom-in' results (58.6% ScreenSpot-Pro, 62.2% OSWorld-G) are prominently featured in Table 1 and Table 3 and the abstract, but involve two-pass test-time computation without extra training — no comparable zoom/crop stage is given to baselines (e.g., GUI-Actor or JEDI with the same two-step inference), so the headline 'state-of-the-art' claim partly rests on an inference-time advantage unavailable to competitors.

Only one backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) is evaluated; the claim that the method aligns 'intrinsic multimodal attention' of MLLMs generally would be better supported by results on a second backbone or scale (e.g., 7B), especially given the method is explicitly designed to be architecture-agnostic.

The claimed preservation of general MLLM capabilities (motivating the anchor token in Section 3.3) is never empirically verified — no evaluation of general VQA/captioning performance before and after fine-tuning is reported.

Novelty is incremental relative to TAG and GUI-Actor: the main advances are the anchor-token simplification and head weighting, and some gains are modest (e.g., global top-1 Qs gives +1.90% over uniform weighting in ablations; weighted patch labels +1.26%), so headline improvements over the simplified baseline could be more precisely attributed.

Additional inference overhead is not quantified: computing head weights requires extracting hidden states and attention across all layers/heads, and the two-step inference doubles latency; no cost/runtime comparison with baselines is provided.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the project page link in the abstract is empty and no code or data release is stated; results of most baselines are copied from original papers, and the GUI-G2-3B entry is self-run without details.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('corordinates', 'two-stem inference', 'improvents'), and the relationship between the two reported variants (GUI-AIMA-3B vs. soft) and which one is used for the zoom-in headline result is not clearly stated in Section 4.1.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem (GUI grounding for computer-use agents) with a genuinely interesting mechanism: supervising the intrinsic multi-head self-attention of an MLLM for coordinate-free patch-level grounding, rather than adding external grounding modules or generating coordinates as text. This is a clear, original contribution relative to TAG (training-free, heuristic head selection) and GUI-Actor (extra module with warm-up stage).

The design is well motivated and technically coherent: the <ANCHOR> token as a surrogate aggregator over query tokens simplifies the impractical vanilla aggregation, and the visual-sink query token mechanism (identified via hidden-state similarity rather than per-head attention) provides a principled way to weight attention heads. Appendix A provides supporting analysis that the hidden-state-based pattern differs from per-head attention patterns, justifying this choice.

Strong empirical evidence: state-of-the-art results among 3B models on ScreenSpot-Pro (45.2% base, 58.6% with zoom-in) and OSWorld-G (62.2%), competitive with much larger models (UI-TARS-1.5-7B, JEDI-7B, GUI-Actor-7B), with notable data efficiency (~85k screenshots, 259k instructions, single-stage fine-tuning).

Comprehensive ablations that isolate each design choice (anchor token vs. vanilla aggregation, head weighting with/without visual-sink tokens, global vs. layer-wise Qs selection, soft matching variant, weighted patch-wise labeling), plus a detailed analysis of the two-step zoom-in inference (Table 5) with offset-error statistics, and convergence comparisons (Fig. 4).

The two-step crop-and-zoom-in inference is a natural consequence of the patch-wise formulation and requires no additional training, which is a practical advantage over coordinate-generation approaches.
weaknesses: The method is evaluated on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct). Claims about 'triggering the native grounding capability of MLLMs' and generalization would be substantially strengthened by demonstrating the approach transfers to at least one other MLLM family or scale.

The claim that anchored-attention supervision preserves the MLLM's general capabilities (motivating Section 3.3 via Nguyen et al., 2023) is never empirically validated. No evaluation on general multimodal benchmarks (e.g., captioning, VQA) before/after fine-tuning is reported, leaving a core motivation untested.

Fairness concerns in the headline comparisons: the best reported numbers (58.6% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 62.2% on OSWorld-G) use the two-step zoom-in inference with an extra forward pass and crop, whereas key baselines (e.g., GUI-Actor, JEDI) are compared without such test-time augmentation. The fair one-step comparison (45.2% vs. GUI-Actor-7B 44.6%) is much closer, so the framing overstates the gap.

The practical inference cost of the method is not quantified: extracting and aggregating attention maps across all L×H layers/heads at every step appears memory- and compute-intensive for autoregressive decoding, and no latency/throughput numbers are given despite the efficiency claims.

Several reported gains are small and without statistical significance analysis (e.g., visual-sink head weighting adds 1.90% over uniform weighting on ScreenSpot-Pro; soft patch labeling adds 1.26%), and results on a ~1582-image benchmark could be sensitive to such margins. No seed/variance reporting is provided.

Some methodological details feel ad hoc and only empirically justified: fixed top-1 global Qs selection, alpha=0.8, 448-pixel crop and 2x zoom-in factor; the sensitivity analysis exists only for the zoom factor, not for K, alpha, or crop size.
The project page URL is incomplete in the manuscript, and no explicit code/model release statement is given, which weakens reproducibility given the many implementation-specific choices.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., duplicated phrase 'for grounding' in Section 3.4, 'corordinates', inconsistent zoom-in improvement numbers between Table 1 (58.6) and Table 5 (58.57), unexplained '2-stem' typo), suggesting the paper would benefit from another careful pass.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question: whether the intrinsic attention of MLLMs can be directly specialized for coordinate-free GUI grounding, without extra grounding modules (GUI-Actor) or impractical token-wise aggregation (TAG). The anchored <ANCHOR>-token aggregation and visual-sink query token head-weighting are simple, well-motivated mechanisms.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2), with state-of-the-art results among 3B models (e.g., 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro with zoom-in, 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2) and competitive performance against substantially larger models.

The data-efficiency claim is well supported: GUI-AIMA-3B-lite is trained on a subset of GUI-Actor's data and outperforms it on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v1, providing a controlled comparison; training-time measurements (Table 8) further substantiate the efficiency claims.

Thorough ablations isolate each design choice: vanilla vs. simplified attention grounding, head-weighting strategies (uniform, all-query, anchor-only, visual-sink), global vs. layer-wise token selection, and weighted patch labeling (Table 5), with consistent results on a larger training set in the appendix.

The two-step zoom-in inference is analyzed quantitatively (Table 6), including corrected/lost prediction counts rather than only aggregate accuracy, which is a transparent treatment of the test-time procedure.
The paper is clearly written, with a clean formulation (Eqs. 1-6), good figures, and useful appendices (efficiency, head-weight analysis, ablations, visualizations).
weaknesses: Comparisons in the headline tables are complicated by the zoom-in (two-step) inference, which is a test-time scaling procedure applied to GUI-AIMA variants but not to most baselines. While the one-step numbers are reported, several 'SOTA' claims rely on the zoom-enhanced results, and a more balanced test-time-scaled comparison (e.g., multi-sample or verifier baselines, which are partially included) would strengthen the claims.

All results are on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) with no error bars or repeated runs; the improvements from individual components are sometimes small (e.g., 1.26% from weighted patch labeling, 1.9% from visual-sink head weighting on the 45k setting), so variance is a concern for these specific deltas even if the overall trends are convincing.

The method is heuristic in several places (single global top-1 visual-sink token, fixed crop size/zoom factor, specific Gaussian labeling parameterization), and the sensitivity of the design choices to the backbone or patch grid resolution (28x28 specific to Qwen2.5-VL) is not explored; generalization beyond this family of models is unverified, limiting the strength of the 'native grounding capability' claim.

The GUI-AIMA-3B (full) model adds 250k instructions from GroundCUA (710k total), which is also used to train GroundNext; some cross-model comparisons (e.g., against GTA1-7B, Qwen3-VL) are thus across different data regimes and only qualitatively discussed.

Some presentation issues: the project page URL is empty; there are minor citation irregularities (e.g., a 2026-dated arXiv reference 'UI-Venus-1.5'); baselines marked '-' for missing sub-scores make certain table rows hard to compare; and Figure 4's analysis of 'sink-like' tokens is largely anecdotal.

No discussion of failure modes of the patch-wise attention formulation itself (e.g., very small targets spanning few patches at the 28x28 grid, or multi-region instructions), nor societal-impact discussion, though these are not essential to the contribution.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper positions coordinate-free GUI grounding against text-based coordinate generation and provides a fair comparison of three coordinate-free paradigms (TAG-style vanilla attention, GUI-Actor-style embedding heads, and the proposed anchored attention) under matched training data and backbone, which is a genuinely useful experimental contribution beyond the method itself.

Technically clean method: the <ANCHOR> token provides an elegant way to avoid impractical token-wise attention aggregation while keeping grounding supervision disentangled from pretrained query-token attention, and the visual-sink query-token mechanism for head weighting is a reasonable, interpretable design. The ablations (Table 5, Table 10) carefully isolate each component, including the counterintuitive finding that all-token and <ANCHOR>-only head weighting are worse than the selected subset.

Strong empirical evidence: evaluation on five widely used benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro/v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2) with both SFT and RL baselines, showing SOTA among 3B models (e.g., 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro with zoom-in) with notable data efficiency (509k instructions, one stage, no extra module or warm-up).

Supporting analyses add credibility: convergence comparison (Fig. 5), zoom-in offset-error decomposition (Table 6), head-weight visualization and head-pruning experiment (Sec. 4.5), and inference/training time comparison vs. GUI-Actor (Table 8).
The plug-and-play two-step zoom-in inference is a practical contribution that requires no retraining and is analyzed in detail rather than just reported as a number.
weaknesses: Fairness of headline comparisons: the bolded best results in Tables 1, 3, 4 come from the two-step zoom-in variant, which doubles inference cost and uses a task-specific crop heuristic; some comparisons against single-pass baselines are therefore not cost-matched. The one-step results (53.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro) are also strong, but the abstract and conclusion emphasize the zoom-in numbers.

Potential training/test overlap needs clearer discussion: UI-Vision is described as 'in-domain' for GUI-AIMA-3B, and the model is additionally trained on 250k GroundCUA/GroundNext instructions whose relation to the UI-Vision and ScreenSpot-Pro distributions is not characterized. On UI-Vision (60.0%) the model is far behind GroundNext-3B-RL (62.1%) despite using GroundNext's training data, which the text frames favorably but only via cross-benchmark comparisons.

Novelty is incremental: the core idea (supervising query-visual attention for GUI grounding) is established by TAG and GUI-Actor; the contributions are an anchor-token aggregation variant plus a heuristic head-weighting scheme and a zoom-in inference trick borrowed conceptually from prior test-time-scaling practice. Individual gains from the components are modest (e.g., +1.90% from head weighting, +1.26% from weighted labeling on ScreenSpot-Pro).

Presentation and consistency issues: the project-page link is blank in the abstract; Table 1 lists 'GroundNext-7B (RL)' with a Liu et al. citation while the text attributes it to Feizi et al.; Table 4 is titled 'OSWorld-G-Refine' without the 'Refine' variant being explained; and at least one reference is dated 2026 with a future-looking arXiv ID. These undermine polish and reproducibility confidence.

Results are reported on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) with single runs and no variance estimates; there is no evidence the framework transfers to other base models or larger scales (e.g., a 7B variant), which weakens the generality claims of the 'framework'.

The head-weighting mechanism has a small dynamic range (Fig. 6 weights ~0.0015–0.003 after softmax over L·H), and the stop-gradient ablation (Table 10) suggests the weights matter mostly at inference; the training-dynamics role of w is not fully explained, and details like the choice of K=1 and global layer sharing, while ablated, are somewhat heuristic.
Societal impact and failure analysis are limited; the limitations discussion is essentially absent beyond a one-sentence future-work note.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper convincingly argues for coordinate-free GUI grounding via intrinsic attention, positioning itself precisely relative to TAG (tuning-free, vanilla aggregation) and GUI-Actor (extra grounding module + warm-up stage), and the <ANCHOR>-token design that sidesteps impractical token-wise aggregation is a simple, elegant, and technically sound contribution.

The visual-sink query token mechanism (Eq. 3-5) for adaptive attention-head weighting is a thoughtful and original design; it is well justified both intuitively and empirically (Fig. 4, Appendix C, and the head-pruning analysis in Sec. 4.5 showing w_{l,h} meaningfully ranks grounding-relevant heads).

Comprehensive empirical evidence: five benchmarks spanning desktop, mobile, and web; three baseline categories (general MLLMs, SFT, RL); and careful ablations (45k and 259k settings) that isolate each component: anchored aggregation (+2.7% over vanilla), head weighting with Q_s (+1.9%), and overlap/distance-aware labeling (+1.26%) on ScreenSpot-Pro.

Strong data-efficiency claims are supported: GUI-AIMA-3B-lite, trained on a subset of GUI-Actor's data, already reaches 49.8% on ScreenSpot-Pro (vs. 42.2 for GUI-Actor-3B), and training-time comparison (Table 8) substantiates the efficiency argument (~192 vs. ~260 A100-hours).

The two-step zoom-in inference is a genuinely plug-and-play contribution that requires no additional training, and Sec. 4.4 provides a detailed error-decomposition analysis (corrected vs. lost predictions, sensitivity to zoom factor) rather than just reporting headline gains.
Efficient attention-map extraction (eager attention only for grounding-relevant rows, ~4.2% overhead) shows practical engineering care, and the paper is generally well written and clearly organized.
weaknesses: All main results and all ablations use a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B). Given the central claim that the method 'triggers the native grounding capability of MLLMs,' results on at least one other backbone (different scale or family) would substantially strengthen the generality claim; GUI-AIMA-7B is notably absent.

A large fraction of the headline gains comes from the two-step zoom-in inference rather than the core attention-supervision contribution (e.g., ScreenSpot-Pro 53.8 -> 61.5, UI-Vision 27.9 -> 60.0 for the lite variant). This is legitimate, but the framing occasionally blends training-time contributions and inference-time scaling, making the core method's standalone advantage harder to disentangle; two-step inference also doubles inference latency, which is only partially addressed.

The UI-Vision comparison is somewhat unfavorable (60.0 vs. 62.1 for GroundNext-3B RL, in-domain for both) and the paper acknowledges it only briefly; the training data (250k GroundCUA instructions) is shared with GroundNext's training data, raising questions about how the comparison should be interpreted.

Reproducibility is currently weak: the project page link in the abstract is empty, and no code or training configuration release is stated. For a framework with many small design choices (top-1 vs. layer-wise Q_s, alpha=0.8 Gaussian labeling, crop size 616, 2x zoom), code release matters considerably.

Several references appear unreliable or incorrectly cited (e.g., 'UI-venus-1.5' with arXiv:2602.09082 dated 2026, duplicated GTA1/InfiGUI entries with inconsistent author lists), which raises concerns about citation hygiene and needs correction.

Some ablation margins are small and would benefit from variance reporting or multiple seeds (e.g., the 1.26% gain from weighted patch-wise labeling, and the close competition among head-weighting variants in Table 5).

The paper does not discuss failure modes or limitations of the attention-based formulation itself (e.g., behavior with multi-target instructions, ambiguous queries, or when intrinsic attention is genuinely absent), despite mentioning multi-region grounding as future work only in the appendix.
